title: pkix-difftest: apply PKITS initial policy inputs to the oracles
description:
PkitsVector parses four RFC 5280 §6.1.1 initial inputs from vectors.json and no oracle applies any of them:

  initial_policy_set
  initial_policy_mapping_inhibit
  initial_explicit_policy
  initial_any_policy_inhibit

The pkix-path oracle builds a bare ValidationPolicy::new(now) (pkix-difftest/src/oracles/pkix_path.rs:110). A grep across the crate finds these fields nowhere outside the struct definition. They are pub fields on a pub struct, so dead-code analysis never objected.

35 of 249 PKITS vectors ask for non-default inputs:
  11  NIST-test-policy-1
   9  NIST-test-policy-2
   3  anyPolicy + initial_explicit_policy
   2  NIST-test-policy-1 + explicit
   2  [policy-1, policy-2] + explicit
   2  anyPolicy + policy_mapping_inhibit
   2  NIST-test-policy-6
   1  NIST-test-policy-2 + explicit
   1  NIST-test-policy-3
   1  [policy-1, policy-2]
   1  anyPolicy + any_policy_inhibit

PKITS §4.8/§4.10/§4.12 drive one bundle repeatedly under different inputs; the '(Subpart N)' suffixes ARE those repeats. should_validate is the expected result under the vector's inputs, so comparing a default-settings verdict against it scores a harness limitation as the implementation disagreeing with NIST. That is what it was doing: 13 of 15 baseline ground_truth_disagreements were policy vectors, every one of them §4.8, §4.10 or §4.12.

Interim fix shipped: the PKITS loader withholds ground truth (expected: None) for vectors whose inputs it cannot honour, which classify() already handles. 15 ground-truth disagreements became 2, and both of those are real. Cross-oracle classification is unchanged and still meaningful, since every oracle gets the same default inputs.

The real fix is to supply the inputs. pkix-path supports all four directly as ValidationPolicy fields, so for that oracle it is plumbing: carry them on Chain, populate from PkitsVector, set them in the oracle.

The hard part is the other two oracles, and it needs a decision rather than code:
- openssl CLI has -policy, -explicit_policy, -policy_check, -inhibit_map, -inhibit_any, so it can probably comply.
- pyca PolicyBuilder likely cannot express an initial policy set at all.

Applying inputs to pkix-path alone would make pkix-path correct against ground truth while leaving the cross-oracle comparison apples-to-oranges, moving chains into Looser/StricterThanWild for no real reason. So either every oracle honours them, or a per-oracle 'cannot honour these inputs' marker keeps the non-compliant ones out of that chain's comparison.

Found while working PKIX-vcpy.
close_reason:
Fixed in 3e9bd47c (wiring) and 7c1a74c5 (the sweep that scores it).

InitialPolicyInputs rides on Chain, defaulting to RFC 5280 §6.1.1's own defaults so a corpus that does not vary them needs no opinion and an oracle can honour it unconditionally. The PKITS loader populates it from the four Initial* fields, resolving anyPolicy and the NIST test policy names to OIDs under 2.16.840.1.101.3.2.1.48 and failing on an unknown name rather than quietly validating under a policy set that omits it. The pkix-path oracle sets all four on ValidationPolicy.

Ground truth restored for all 249. Reverting the wiring puts back exactly 13 disagreements -- the count this bead recorded as policy vectors -- so the fix is confirmed against the baseline it was measured from.

Took the per-oracle marker, the second of the two options in the bead, because pyca's PolicyBuilder cannot express a user-initial-policy-set at all, which rules out 'every oracle honours them'. OracleName::honours_policy_inputs gates voting: an oracle that cannot express the inputs is skipped for any chain whose inputs are not the defaults, so cross-oracle comparison only ever compares oracles asked the same question, and costs nothing on the 214 default-input vectors or on any other corpus. Ground truth is scored per oracle, so pkix-path is unaffected.

openssl is still unwired. It has -policy, -explicit_policy, -policy_check, -inhibit_map and -inhibit_any, so it could probably comply; that is now an improvement to cross-oracle coverage rather than a correctness gap, since nothing is scored wrongly while it abstains. Not filed as a separate bead -- the capability method documents it at the decision point.

Result: 246 of 249 vectors agree with NIST. The 3 that do not are PKIX-vb4o (DSA, 4.1.4 and 4.1.5) and PKIX-2kgd (4.2.3, notBefore 1950 below der's 1970 floor), both recorded as exemptions that fail the test if they start passing.
